name: What Is Food Security and Why Is It Needed?

scenes.animation: A kirana shop shelf is fully stocked with rice, wheat and dal. A labourer walks in, counts a few coins, and walks out with only a tiny packet. Zippy looks from the full shelf to the tiny packet, confused.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The shop is full of food, but he couldn't buy enough. So is there food, or isn't there?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's exactly why food security has more than one part. Having food in the country isn't enough.

scenes.animation: Three pillars rise under a roof labelled 'Food Security'. Pillar 1: 'Availability: production, imports, stock in government granaries'. Pillar 2: 'Accessibility: food within reach of every person'. Pillar 3: 'Affordability: enough money to buy sufficient, safe and nutritious food'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Food security means availability, accessibility and affordability of food to all people at all times.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Availability means food production within the country, food imports, and the previous years' stock stored in government granaries.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Accessibility means food is within reach of every person. Affordability means an individual has enough money to buy sufficient, safe and nutritious food to meet dietary needs.

scenes.animation: A drought cracks a field; a cyclone sweeps a coast. Food shelves empty and a price tag balloons upwards. Arrows lead to a grim label 'Famine: widespread deaths due to starvation and epidemics'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Why is it needed? The poorest are food insecure most of the time. But during a calamity like drought, earthquake or tsunami, even people above the poverty line can become food insecure.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Production falls, prices rise, and some people cannot afford food. If the calamity lasts, it can lead to starvation. A massive situation of starvation might turn into a famine.

scenes.animation: A sepia map of undivided Bengal with the label '1943: The Great Bengal Famine'. A counter rises to '30 lakh deaths'. Silhouettes appear with labels 'Agricultural labourers', 'Fishermen', 'Transport workers', 'Casual labourers'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The most devastating famine in India was the Famine of Bengal in 1943. It killed thirty lakh people in the province of Bengal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The most affected were agricultural labourers, fishermen, transport workers and other casual labourers.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Thirty lakh. That's a whole city's worth of people.

scenes.animation: A timeline rolls forward from 1943 to today with the caption 'No famine since then'. But a small warning icon remains: 'Hunger still exists'. An 'EXAM TIP' card highlights 'Availability, Accessibility, Affordability'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No famine of that scale has occurred in India since then. But hunger and food insecurity still exist in some areas.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: always define food security with its three dimensions. Missing even one costs you marks.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three pillars: '1. Food security = availability + accessibility + affordability', '2. Calamities can make even non-poor food insecure', '3. Bengal Famine, 1943: 30 lakh deaths'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: food security means availability, accessibility and affordability of food for all, at all times.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: natural calamities can push even the non-poor into food insecurity.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the Bengal Famine of 1943 killed thirty lakh people.

name: Who Are Food Insecure? Chronic and Seasonal Hunger

scenes.animation: Monsoon clouds over an empty village field. A farm labourer sits idle outside his hut, counting days on a calendar. Zippy sits beside him with an empty tiffin box.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: He works hard during the harvest. Why is his family hungry now?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because farm work is seasonal. No work means no wages, and no wages means not enough food.

scenes.animation: A panel of rural and urban groups lights up. Rural: 'Landless people with little or no land', 'Traditional artisans', 'Providers of traditional services', 'Petty self-employed workers', 'Destitutes, including beggars'. Urban: 'Families in ill-paid occupations and casual labour'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Worst affected in rural areas are landless people, traditional artisans, providers of traditional services, petty self-employed workers and destitutes, including beggars.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In urban areas, the food insecure are families whose working members are generally employed in ill-paid occupations and the casual labour market.

scenes.animation: More groups appear: 'SC, ST and some OBC with poor land base', 'People affected by natural disasters', 'Pregnant and nursing mothers', 'Children under 5'. Then a map of India shades the most food-insecure regions: 'Uttar Pradesh (eastern and south-eastern parts), Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh, parts of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Scheduled castes, scheduled tribes and some sections of the other backward classes with poor land base are also prone to food insecurity. So are people affected by natural disasters.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Pregnant and nursing mothers and children under the age of five form an important segment of the food insecure population.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Food insecure people are mostly found in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh, and parts of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.

scenes.animation: Split screen. Left: 'Chronic hunger': a plate stays half-empty on every day of the calendar. Right: 'Seasonal hunger': the plate is full in harvest months and empty in lean months, with a farm calendar and an urban casual worker waiting at a labour chowk.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Hunger has two dimensions. Chronic hunger is a consequence of diets persistently inadequate in quantity or quality. Poor people suffer from it because of their very low income.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Seasonal hunger is related to cycles of food growing and harvesting. It is prevalent in rural areas because farm work is seasonal, and in urban areas because of casual labour.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So chronic is always, seasonal is sometimes.

scenes.animation: A table with two columns, 'Chronic' and 'Seasonal', fills with one example each. An 'EXAM TIP' card flips over.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: when asked to distinguish chronic and seasonal hunger, give the cause of each: persistent low income versus seasonal lack of work.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a half-plate icon: '1. Rural landless, artisans, destitutes; urban casual labour', '2. SC, ST, some OBC; disaster victims; mothers and children under 5', '3. Chronic hunger (persistent) vs seasonal hunger (cycles of work)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: landless labourers, artisans, destitutes and urban casual workers are most food insecure.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: socially disadvantaged groups, disaster victims, and mothers and young children are also at risk.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: chronic hunger is persistent, while seasonal hunger follows the cycles of work.

name: Self-Sufficiency in Foodgrains and the Buffer Stock

scenes.animation: A giant warehouse labelled 'FCI' with tall stacks of wheat and rice sacks. Zippy peeks in, his eyes widening, and shouts 'Hello!'; the echo bounces around.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Who keeps so much grain, and why?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The government does. It's India's safety net against hunger. But first, let's see how India became self-sufficient in foodgrains.

scenes.animation: A sepia 1960s field transforms into a golden wheat field with HYV seed packets. A postage stamp is animated being printed: 'Wheat Revolution, July 1968', with a caption 'Released by Indira Gandhi'. Punjab and Haryana glow brightest on the map.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After Independence, India adopted a new strategy in agriculture, which resulted in the Green Revolution, especially in the production of wheat and rice.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Indira Gandhi, then Prime Minister, officially recorded the impressive strides of the Green Revolution by releasing a special stamp, entitled Wheat Revolution, in July 1968.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The highest growth was seen in Punjab and Haryana. Since then, India has become self-sufficient in foodgrains.

scenes.animation: A flowchart builds step by step: 'Farmers in surplus states' → 'FCI procures wheat and rice at Minimum Support Price (announced before sowing)' → 'Stored in granaries = Buffer stock' → 'Distributed in deficit areas and among the poor at Issue Price'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Buffer stock is the stock of foodgrains, namely wheat and rice, procured by the government through the Food Corporation of India.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The FCI purchases wheat and rice from farmers in states where there is surplus production. Farmers are paid a pre-announced price called the Minimum Support Price. It is declared by the government every year before the sowing season to encourage production.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The grain is stored in granaries and distributed in deficit areas and among the poorer strata at a price lower than the market price, called the Issue Price.

scenes.animation: A see-saw: drought pushes one side down, and a crane lifts sacks from the FCI warehouse to balance it. A label reads 'Buffer stock solves shortage during adverse weather or calamity'. An 'EXAM TIP' card appears with 'MSP' and 'Issue Price' side by side.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the buffer stock is like my emergency snack drawer?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. It helps resolve the problem of food shortage during adverse weather conditions or times of calamity.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: MSP is paid to farmers; Issue Price is charged to buyers. Students often mix them up.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a wheat stamp and warehouse icon: '1. Green Revolution: 'Wheat Revolution' stamp, July 1968', '2. FCI procures at MSP → buffer stock', '3. Distributed at Issue Price in deficit areas'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the Green Revolution made India self-sufficient in foodgrains.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the FCI buys wheat and rice at the Minimum Support Price to create a buffer stock.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: this grain reaches deficit areas and the poor at the lower Issue Price.

name: The Public Distribution System and the Role of Cooperatives

scenes.animation: A queue outside a small shop labelled 'Fair Price Shop / Ration Shop'. A mother shows a ration card and receives rice, wheat and sugar at low prices. Zippy holds a school ID card and gets politely turned away.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why doesn't my card work here?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because this shop needs a ration card. Welcome to the Public Distribution System.

scenes.animation: A network map spreads from FCI godowns to thousands of small shop icons across India. Labels: 'PDS: food procured by FCI distributed through ration shops', 'Items: foodgrains, sugar, kerosene for cooking'. Three cards fan out: 'Antyodaya card: poorest of the poor', 'BPL card: below poverty line', 'APL card: all others'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The food procured by the FCI is distributed among the poorer sections through government-regulated ration shops. This is called the Public Distribution System, or PDS.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ration shops, also known as fair price shops, keep stock of foodgrains, sugar and kerosene for cooking, sold at a price lower than the market price.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: There are three kinds of ration cards: Antyodaya cards for the poorest of the poor, BPL cards for those below the poverty line, and APL cards for all others.

scenes.animation: A timeline builds: '1992: Revamped PDS in 1,700 blocks', '1997: Targeted PDS', 'December 2000: Antyodaya Anna Yojana, one crore poorest BPL families, 25 kg per family, wheat ₹2/kg, rice ₹3/kg; later raised to 35 kg', '2013: National Food Security Act'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1992, the Revamped Public Distribution System was introduced in one thousand seven hundred blocks. In 1997, the Targeted PDS followed, with different prices for poor and non-poor.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Antyodaya Anna Yojana was launched in December 2000 for one crore of the poorest BPL families. Each family got twenty-five kilograms of foodgrains at two rupees a kilo for wheat and three rupees for rice. The quantity was later raised to thirty-five kilograms.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The National Food Security Act, 2013, provides food and nutritional security, and covers seventy-five per cent of the rural and fifty per cent of the urban population.

scenes.animation: Three cooperative badges appear on a map: 'Tamil Nadu: about 94% of fair price shops run by cooperatives', 'Delhi: Mother Dairy, milk and vegetables at controlled rates', 'Gujarat: Amul, White Revolution'. A fourth badge in Maharashtra: 'ADS: network of NGOs setting up grain banks'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Cooperatives also play an important role, especially in southern and western India. In Tamil Nadu, around ninety-four per cent of fair price shops are run by cooperatives.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Delhi, Mother Dairy provides milk and vegetables at controlled rates. Amul in Gujarat brought about the White Revolution in the country. In Maharashtra, the Academy of Development Science helped a network of NGOs set up grain banks.

scenes.animation: A PDS report card shows some complaints: 'Poor quality grain', 'Irregular opening of shops', 'Dealers diverting grain'. An 'EXAM TIP' card highlights 'AAY: December 2000'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Is the PDS perfect then?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not always. Ration dealers sometimes divert grain to the open market, sell poor quality grain or open shops irregularly. Exam tip: the functioning of PDS and the role of cooperatives are frequent long-answer questions.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a ration card icon: '1. PDS: ration shops; Antyodaya, BPL, APL cards', '2. RPDS 1992, TPDS 1997, AAY 2000, NFSA 2013', '3. Cooperatives: Tamil Nadu shops, Mother Dairy, Amul, ADS grain banks'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the PDS supplies subsidised food through ration shops using three kinds of cards.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: schemes evolved from RPDS in 1992 to TPDS, Antyodaya Anna Yojana, and the Food Security Act of 2013.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: cooperatives like Mother Dairy, Amul and grain banks strengthen food security.
